Pouch urine growing low-concentration Pseudomonas aeruginosa on day 7 represents reservoir colonisation, a recognised contributor to chronic inflammation and weakening of the reservoir wall predisposing to rupture.

DECISIVE IMAGING: Urgent contrast CT with retrograde pouch contrast (pouchography) demonstrated a large left laterodorsal reservoir wall defect with contrast leakage into the peritoneal cavity and free intraperitoneal fluid — pathognomonic for intraperitoneal pouch rupture with urinary ascites.

DEFINITIVE CONFIRMATION: Emergency exploratory laparotomy confirmed pouch rupture, which was primarily repaired, with re-siting and secure fixation of the pouch catheter and nasogastric decompression.

DIFFERENTIALS EXCLUDED: (1) Urosepsis/septic shock — excluded by normal pre-operative CRP, negative blood cultures and immediate mechanical findings on CT. (2) Simple catheter blockage with reservoir over-distension alone — excluded by demonstrated transmural defect and intraperitoneal contrast leak. (3) Bowel perforation/pneumoperitoneum — not supported; contrast extravasation was from the reservoir, and no free gas was reported. (4) Obstructive acute kidney injury from bilateral ureteric obstruction — excluded by normal creatinine and eGFR. (5) Primary cardiopulmonary cause of dyspnoea (PE, MI, pneumonia) — the dyspnoea was secondary to diaphragmatic splinting from urinary ascites and resolved with surgical decompression and repair.

CONCLUSION: The unifying diagnosis is spontaneous intraperitoneal rupture of a continent urinary reservoir precipitated by catheter drainage failure, presenting as an acute surgical abdomen with urinary ascites, chemical peritonitis and secondary cardiopulmonary decompensation, requiring emergency laparotomy and repair.
